Pattern Matching -- Inventing Wildcards and Regular Expressions

When you type *.txt in a file browser, or validate an email address on a signup form, or grep through a server log -- a pattern matcher is at work. In this chapter you will invent one from scratch: first exact matching, then the ? wildcard, then the surprisingly deep * wildcard (a beautiful use of the recursion you already own), and finally you will graduate to Python's industrial-strength re module and mine a real web-server log with it.

Navigate: press → or Space to advance  |  ← to go back

Challenge (skip ahead if you can):

Write a glob-style matcher. Given a pattern and a text, return True only if the whole text matches. In the pattern, ? matches exactly one character, * matches any sequence (including empty), and every other character matches itself.

def match(pattern, text):
    # your code here
    ...
match("cat", "cat")          # True
match("c?t", "cut")          # True
match("*.txt", "notes.txt")  # True
match("a*b*c", "aXXbYc")     # True
match("a*b", "abc")          # False

Bonus: do the same job with Python's re module. What regex would you use to find every date like 2024-03-15 in a log file?

Already got it? The next slides will guide you step by step.

Part 1: Exact Match

Character by Character

Write match_exact(pat, text) that returns True only when the pattern and the text are exactly the same -- without using == on whole strings. Compare one character at a time.

Why the restriction? Because in a moment some pattern characters will stop meaning themselves -- and then whole-string == is useless. Build the loop (or recursion) now, while the problem is easy.

Think recursively: two strings match if their first characters match and the rest of them match. What are the base cases?

match_exact("abc", "abc")    # True
match_exact("abc", "abd")    # False
match_exact("abc", "abcd")   # False
match_exact("", "")          # True
Hint 1

Think about the base cases first. When are two strings definitely equal? When are they definitely not? What if one is empty and the other is not?

Hint 2

Base case 1: both strings are empty → return True. Base case 2: one is empty and the other is not → return False.

Hint 3

Recursive case: if pat[0] == text[0], return match_exact(pat[1:], text[1:]). Otherwise return False.

Part 2: The `?` Wildcard

New rule: in the pattern, ? matches exactly one character -- any character.

a?  matches: a1, a2, aa, ax
a?  does not match: a, abc

Add `?` to Your Matcher

Write match_q(pat, text). It is match_exact with one extra case: when the first pattern character is ?, what should you compare -- and what do you recurse on?

match_q("a?c", "abc")    # True
match_q("a?c", "axc")    # True
match_q("a?c", "ac")     # False
match_q("???", "xyz")    # True
Hint 1

Start from your match_exact code. You only need to add one new check: when pat[0] is '?', what should happen?

Hint 2

When pat[0] == '?', you do not need to check whether pat[0] == text[0] — the ? matches any character. Just make sure the text is not empty, then recurse on the rest.

Hint 3

If pat[0] == '?' and len(text) > 0: return match_q(pat[1:], text[1:]). All other cases stay the same as match_exact.

Part 3: The `*` Wildcard

The big one: * matches zero or more characters -- any characters.

a*     matches: a, ab, abc, ax
a*b    matches: ab, axyzb, a123b
a*b*c  matches: abc, abbbc, a1b1c
aa?b*  matches: aa1b, aaxby, aa1bcdeffgshshshsh
aa?b*  does not match: aab, ab

Think Before You Code

Pattern a*b, text "axyzb". The a matches. Now the pattern says * and the text says "xyzb". How many characters should the * swallow?

You cannot know yet -- it depends on what comes after the star. So don't decide. Try both options and let recursion explore:

  1. The * swallows nothing --> try matching the rest of the pattern (b) against "xyzb".
  2. The * swallows one more character --> the star stays, try *b against "yzb".

If either branch succeeds, the match succeeds. What is the base case when the text runs out but the pattern is "*"?

Hint 1

When you see * at pat[0], use Python's or to try both branches: match(pat[1:], text) or match(pat, text[1:]).

Hint 2

Be careful with the second branch — you can only swallow a character from text if text is not empty. So the second branch needs a guard: len(text) > 0 and match(pat, text[1:]).

The Full Matcher

Write match(pat, text) supporting literals, ?, and *.

Hint 1

Combine the logic from match_exact, match_q, and the * branching you just worked out. Handle * first, then ?, then literal characters.

Hint 2

Base cases: (1) both empty → True. (2) pattern is only *s and text is empty → True (a star can match nothing). (3) pattern empty but text not → False.

Hint 3 (near-giveaway) 
def match(pat, text):
    if not pat:
        return not text
    if pat[0] == '*':
        # star matches nothing OR one more char
        return match(pat[1:], text) or (len(text) > 0 and match(pat, text[1:]))
    if not text:
        return False
    if pat[0] == '?' or pat[0] == text[0]:
        return match(pat[1:], text[1:])
    return False

Use It Like a Shell

Your match is exactly what the shell does with filenames (called globbing).

Write find_matching(pattern, names) that returns all names matching the pattern.

files = ["report.txt", "report.pdf", "data1.csv", "data2.csv", "notes.txt", "img.png"]
find_matching("*.txt", files)      # ["report.txt", "notes.txt"]
find_matching("data?.csv", files)  # ["data1.csv", "data2.csv"]
find_matching("report.*", files)   # ["report.txt", "report.pdf"]
Hint 1

This is a one-liner: loop through names and keep only those where match(pattern, name) returns True.

Hint 2

Use a list comprehension: [name for name in names if match(pattern, name)].

Quick Check 3.1 -- Why `*` Needs Backtracking

The pattern a*b is matched against the string axxbyyb. The * is greedy -- it first tries to consume as many characters as possible. Why does the matcher need backtracking to find the correct match?

A. Because * can only match letters, not x or y

B. The greedy * initially consumes xxbyyb, but then the final b in the pattern has nothing left to match -- so the matcher must back up and try consuming fewer characters

C. Backtracking is needed because the string contains duplicate b characters

D. The pattern is invalid -- * must be at the end

Answer: B. The * greedily eats everything, but then the b at the end of the pattern has no characters left to match. The matcher must "back up" (backtrack) and let the * consume fewer characters until the remaining pattern can match.

Part 4: Regular Expressions -- The Professional Version

What you invented is the core idea behind regular expressions -- a pattern language so useful it is built into every programming language. Python's re module speaks a richer dialect:

.        any single character            (your ?)
*        previous thing, 0 or more times (your * -- but attached to what precedes it!)
+        previous thing, 1 or more times
[aeiou]  any ONE character from the set
[0-9]    any ONE digit (ranges work)
[^xyz]   any ONE character NOT in the set
{4}      previous thing, exactly 4 times
\.       a literal dot (backslash = escape)
^  $     start / end of the line

Note the twist: regex * means "repeat the previous item" -- so ab*c matches ac, abc, abbbc. Your glob-style a*b is written a.*b in regex.

The two functions you need:

import re
re.search(pattern, text)    # a match object if found anywhere in text, else None
re.findall(pattern, text)   # list of every match in the text

Quick Demo

Try these in a Python shell to see re.search and re.findall in action:

import re

# search returns the first match (or None)
m = re.search(r"[0-9]+", "I have 42 apples and 7 oranges")
print(m.group())   # "42"

# findall returns every match as a list
re.findall(r"[0-9]+", "I have 42 apples and 7 oranges")
# ["42", "7"]

# .  means any character;  +  means one or more of the previous thing
re.findall(r"a.+e", "apple and orange")
# ["apple and orange"]  -- the .+ is greedy!

r"..." is a raw string -- it tells Python not to treat backslashes specially. Always use raw strings for regex patterns.

Match Dates

Dates appear as 05/07/1980 or 05-07-1980 (day, month, year -- separator is / or -).

Write a regex string DATE_PATTERN so that re.search(DATE_PATTERN, line) finds dates. Start simple: two digits, a separator, two digits, a separator, four digits.

re.search(DATE_PATTERN, "Date: 05/07/1980")   # found
re.search(DATE_PATTERN, "Date: 05-07-1980")   # found
re.search(DATE_PATTERN, "hello world")        # None
Hint 1

Two digits is [0-9]{2} (or \d{2}). Four digits is [0-9]{4}. A separator that is either / or - is the set [/-].

Hint 2

DATE_PATTERN = r"[0-9]{2}[/-][0-9]{2}[/-][0-9]{4}"

Valid Dates Only

Your pattern happily matches 99/88/1980. Tighten it:

  • Day 01--31: can you express it as alternatives? 0[1-9] covers 01--09, [12][0-9] covers 10--29... what covers 30 and 31? Join alternatives with |.
  • Month 01--12: same game.

Group alternatives in parentheses: (0[1-9]|...).

Write STRICT_DATE that matches valid day/month combinations only.

is_valid_date("05/07/1980")   # True
is_valid_date("99/07/1980")   # False   (day 99)
is_valid_date("05/19/1980")   # False   (month 19)
is_valid_date("00/04/1980")   # False   (day 00)

(Don't chase February 30th -- even real-world validators leave calendar logic out of regex.)

Hint 1

Use | (or) inside parentheses to express alternatives. Day: (0[1-9]|[12][0-9]|3[01]). Now do the same for month (01--12).

Hint 2

Month: (0[1-9]|1[0-2]). Glue them together with a separator [/-] and a four-digit year [0-9]{4}. Use ^ and $ anchors so the entire string must match.

Find Credit Card Numbers

A security audit: find credit-card-like numbers (four groups of 4 digits, separated by spaces, dashes, or nothing) leaking into text.

Write find_card_numbers(text) returning the list of matches.

find_card_numbers("cc: 1234-4567-8909-1111 and 1234 4567 8909 1111 and 1234456789091111")
# ["1234-4567-8909-1111", "1234 4567 8909 1111", "1234456789091111"]
Hint 1

A group-plus-separator is [0-9]{4}[- ]? (4 digits followed by an optional space or dash). How many times does that repeat before the last group?

Hint 2

Three groups with an optional separator, then a final group of 4 digits: r"[0-9]{4}[- ]?[0-9]{4}[- ]?[0-9]{4}[- ]?[0-9]{4}". Use re.findall to collect all matches.

Extract Email Addresses

Write find_emails(text) that extracts things shaped like email addresses: one-or-more "word characters" (letters, digits, ., _), then @, then a domain with at least one dot.

find_emails("Contact sandeep@example.com or admin.team@my-site.org today")
# ["sandeep@example.com", "admin.team@my-site.org"]

(A regex that matches every legal email is famously monstrous -- the pragmatic version you are writing is what real codebases actually use.)

Hint 1

"Word characters" in regex are [a-zA-Z0-9._] (or you can use [\w.]). The @ is a literal. The domain has letters, digits, dots, and dashes.

Hint 2

Try: r"[\w.]+@[\w.-]+\.[a-zA-Z]{2,}". The \.[a-zA-Z]{2,} at the end ensures at least one dot in the domain with a two-or-more-letter ending (like .com or .org).

  1. Write find_urls(text) that extracts every http://... or https://... URL. Look closely at the lines: a URL ends where whitespace, a quote ", or a closing parenthesis ) begins -- a negated set [^...] handles all three.
  2. Run it over LOG_LINES and count which domain appears most (your group_by / word-count instincts from the Dictionaries chapter apply).

Part B -- domain_counts:

Write domain_counts(urls) that extracts the domain from each URL and counts how many times each domain appears.

Hint 1 (find_urls)

A URL starts with http:// or https:// and continues until whitespace, a quote, or a closing parenthesis. Try: r"https?://[^\s\"')]+".

Quick Check 4.1 -- Greedy vs Non-Greedy Matching

Given the HTML string <b>hello</b> and <b>world</b>, what does the regex <b>.*</b> match?

A. Just <b>hello</b>

B. Both <b>hello</b> and <b>world</b> as two separate matches

C. The entire string <b>hello</b> and <b>world</b> as one match, because .* is greedy

D. Nothing -- the regex is invalid

Answer: C. The .* is greedy -- it eats as many characters as possible, so it stretches all the way from the first <b> to the last </b>. To match each bold section separately, use .*? (non-greedy): the ? after * means "match as few characters as possible."

What You Just Invented

Your concept What you built Standard name / idea
Exact match match_exact String comparison / recursive decomposition
? wildcard match_q Single-character wildcard (glob ?, regex .)
* wildcard match Star wildcard / backtracking search
Globbing find_matching Shell glob expansion (fnmatch)
Regex patterns re.search / re.findall Regular expressions (Python re module)
Log mining find_urls, domain_counts Text extraction / data wrangling

What you just invented: The branching trick in your * matcher -- try both, succeed if either succeeds -- is called backtracking. It is the same idea that solves mazes, Sudoku, and the N-Queens problem, and it is exactly how simple regex engines are implemented.

Part 5: Reflection -- What Did You Just Build?

Reflection

Take a moment to answer these questions in your own words.

  1. Your match_exact function compares strings character by character using recursion. Why did we build it this way instead of just using ==? What does this approach make possible that == cannot do?
  2. When you added the * wildcard, you had to try two options at every step: "the star swallows nothing" and "the star swallows one more character." Why can't you just decide up front how many characters the star should eat?
  3. Your glob-style * means "match anything." In regex, * means "repeat the previous thing zero or more times." Why is the regex version more precise? Give an example where the difference matters.
  4. In the server-log exercise, you combined regex (find_urls) with dictionary counting (domain_counts). How would you explain this two-step approach to a friend: "first _____, then _____"?
  5. Where else in everyday life do you see pattern matching? Think of at least two examples outside of programming.
